source_user: A long-context workload intermittently hits OOM after several concurrent requests. Give a prioritized diagnosis and mitigations. Scenario variant 17: include an explicit falsifiable hypothesis and a controlled experiment.
source_assistant: Answer should state assumptions, a falsifiable hypothesis, measurements, expected confounders, and rollback criteria. Minimum technical points: measure per-request KV growth and allocator fragmentation; check max sequence and batch; inspect active sequences; test paged/prefix cache, admission control, quantization, and context limits.
corrected_answer:
For scenario variant 17, treat the OOM as a symptom rather than proof of a single cause, and preserve a known-good baseline before changing limits. Record model/build, precision, GPU type/count and capacity, runtime/driver, allocator, KV layout and page size, scheduler, batch/context caps, prefix-cache and admission settings, and the exact request trace. Report bytes versus tokens and allocated versus reserved memory separately; label estimates.

Falsifiable hypothesis: with a fixed configuration and workload stratum, peak device allocation is explained by a fixed model/workspace overhead plus a stable slope against live KV tokens (including both K and V), and memory returns to a prespecified tolerance after requests finish. Falsify this if the slope changes without a configuration change, residual allocated/reserved memory grows after live requests and KV fall to baseline, or an allocation fails while aggregate free memory is sufficient because of fragmentation. Also test the competing hypotheses of an unexpectedly high sequence/batch ceiling, leaked KV after cancellation/timeouts/retries, prefix-cache retention, or host/device accounting error.

Diagnosis and controlled experiment:
1. Capture per-request admission, start/end/cancel/retry timestamps; prompt and generated-token counts; active sequences, batch composition, KV pages/capacity, cache hits/evictions, allocation sizes/failures, allocated/reserved/free device memory, fragmentation/segments, workspace, host-pinned memory, and OOM stack. Sample before, during, and after a request drain. Check whether max sequence length, max batch, retries, or concurrent active sequences exceed the intended envelope.
2. Replay a fixed trace with warm-up and repeated randomized paired runs. Change one factor at a time: concurrency, prompt/output length, batch policy, request lifetime/cancellation, prefix reuse, and context limit. Include short/long and low/high-concurrency strata, and a no-prefix-cache control. Fit a memory-versus-live-KV-token relationship with uncertainty; compare pre-drain peak and post-drain residuals. A correlation alone is not proof of causality.
3. Apply mitigations in reversible order: enforce token-aware admission with headroom and bounded per-request context/output; cap concurrency/batch and reject or queue safely; use paged KV only if its implementation and fragmentation behavior are verified; bound or disable prefix caching if retained pages explain the residue; evaluate KV quantization only after checking accuracy and kernel support; then consider a lower context limit or controlled eviction. Never silently truncate or evict state if it changes correctness.

Success requires no OOM and no correctness regression over repeated representative traces, bounded post-drain residual memory, and prespecified tail-risk/error and latency thresholds with confidence intervals. Define failure denominators for rejected, timed-out, cancelled, and completed requests. Canary one change at limited load, monitor GPU memory/KV/allocator, queue/P99, throughput, error/correctness, and thermal/power signals, and roll back on any OOM, unbounded residual growth, correctness failure, or threshold breach. Do not claim a root cause until the competing controls and evidence support it.

Synthetic traces may not represent production workload tails.
evidence_required: Per-request token/KV/allocation lifecycle traces through drain.
